paragraphs.text: Inspiration is a [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, sold as loose leaf rather than pressed. Nobody recorded the mountain it grew on or the year it was picked, so this page names neither.

Raw pu’er starts as leaf from Yunnan’s large-leaf trees. The leaf is fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), then dried in the sun rather than by hot air, so some of its own activity survives. Kept loose, this tea stays close to [maocha](sheng:processing), the rough tea that other makers press into cakes. That surviving activity is why raw pu’er [keeps changing in storage](sheng:aging) over the years, and why where a tea has been kept becomes part of its history.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
